1.title: Can online friendships be as deep as real ones?
1.brief: Write a discursive essay on whether friendships formed online can be as meaningful as those formed face to face. Present both sides before reaching a nuanced conclusion.
1.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo discursivo sobre si las amistades en línea pueden ser tan profundas como las presenciales.
criteria: Four phrasal verbs used naturally (strike up, fall out, grow on, come across as).
Three gerund and two infinitive constructions, including one perfect infinitive or passive gerund.
Hedged, polite disagreement (I would beg to differ, it could be argued that…).
1.model:
It is often assumed that a friendship struck up online is, by definition, shallower than one forged in a classroom or an office. I would beg to differ, although the question deserves a nuanced answer.

Sceptics argue that digital relationships lack the cues that build trust. Without seeing someone's face, it is easy to come across as warmer, funnier or more confident than one really is. Being deceived by a carefully curated profile is a genuine risk, and many people report feeling let down when an online acquaintance turns out to be quite different in person. Moreover, falling out with someone you have never met is remarkably easy: a single blocked account can end years of conversation.

Yet it could equally be argued that online spaces allow friendships to grow on us in ways that physical proximity does not. Communities built around shared passions, from chess to rare diseases, bring together people who would otherwise never have met. Many claim to have found their closest confidants in such groups, precisely because writing encourages them to open up about things they would struggle to say aloud.

On balance, the medium seems less important than the commitment. A friendship deepens when both people are willing to invest time, to listen and to forgive. Whether that happens over coffee or over a screen, what matters is being on the same wavelength. Online friendships are not inferior; they simply demand a different kind of effort to stand the test of time.

1.title: Burying the hatchet
1.brief: Write an email to a friend you fell out with years ago, proposing a reconciliation. Acknowledge what went wrong without sounding defensive.
1.briefEs: Escribe un correo a un amigo con quien te peleaste hace años proponiendo una reconciliación sin sonar a la defensiva.
criteria: Four phrasal verbs or idioms from the unit, including to bury the hatchet.
A perfect infinitive (seem to have…) and a passive gerund (being left out).
A tone that balances warmth and accountability.
1.model:
Dear Mateo,

I have started this email at least a dozen times, so forgive me if it comes out a little clumsily.

It has been almost four years since we fell out over the business we were planning together, and I have come to realise that I handled the whole situation badly. At the time, I was convinced you had let me down. Looking back, I seem to have ignored how much pressure you were under, and I certainly did nothing to make you feel heard. I remember you saying that you hated being left out of decisions, and you were right: I kept making them without you.

I am not writing to reopen old arguments. I simply miss having you around. We hit it off from the very first week of university, and I don't think I have been on the same wavelength with anyone quite like that since. It seems absurd to have let one failed project end a friendship of ten years.

If you are open to it, I would love to bury the hatchet over a coffee — or a beer, if that feels more appropriate. I'm back in Medellín for the whole of next month, so I could easily fit around your schedule. And if you would rather not, I completely understand; I would still be glad to have finally said this.

Take care, and say hello to your parents for me.

Warmly,
Santiago

1.title: Review: a film about friendship
1.brief: Write a review for a cultural website of a film, series or novel that explores friendship. Analyse how the relationship develops and evaluate how convincingly it is portrayed.
1.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de una película, serie o novela sobre la amistad, analizando cómo evoluciona la relación.
criteria: Four phrasal verbs describing the relationship (hit it off, drift apart, grow on, fall out).
A variety of gerund and infinitive patterns after verbs and adjectives.
Clear evaluation with a final recommendation.
1.model:
The Banshees of Inisherin (2022) begins with one of the most unsettling premises in recent cinema: one morning, Colm simply decides to stop being friends with Pádraic. There is no argument, no betrayal — only Colm's announcement that he no longer wishes to waste his remaining years on dull conversation.

What follows is a darkly comic and ultimately tragic study of what happens when two people drift apart for reasons only one of them understands. Pádraic, played with heartbreaking innocence by Colin Farrell, refuses to accept being cast aside. His attempts to win Colm back grow increasingly desperate, and Colm's determination to be left alone becomes frighteningly extreme.

Director Martin McDonagh avoids explaining too much. We never learn exactly when the two men hit it off or how long their friendship has lasted, yet the film manages to convey decades of shared routine in a few glances. The bleak island landscape seems to have been chosen to mirror their isolation, and the civil war raging across the water is a clever parallel to their private conflict.

The film is not without flaws. Its pace may test viewers who expect a conventional plot, and some of the secondary characters feel underdeveloped. However, the central performances are extraordinary, and the story grows on you long after the credits roll.

I would strongly recommend it to anyone interested in the fragility of adult friendship — though perhaps not as light entertainment for a Friday night.

1.title: Friendship at work: strength or distraction?
1.brief: Write an academic essay assessing whether friendships between colleagues improve or damage workplace performance. State a thesis, weigh the evidence and reach a qualified conclusion.
1.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo académico sobre si las amistades entre compañeros mejoran o perjudican el rendimiento laboral.
criteria: At least four phrasal verbs from the unit (get along with, count on, open up, fall out) with the correct particle and object position.
At least two gerunds and two infinitives, including one perfect infinitive (to have favoured).
A thesis in the first paragraph, hedged claims (tend to, may well) and no contractions.
1.model:
Contemporary organisations increasingly encourage employees to socialise, yet it remains unclear whether workplace friendships help or hinder productivity. This essay argues that, on balance, they are an asset, provided that they are managed with care.

Employees who get along with their colleagues tend to report higher job satisfaction. Being able to count on a trusted peer reduces stress, and people who feel safe are more likely to open up about problems before they become serious. In addition, a friendly atmosphere makes it easier to ask for help. Several studies also suggest that teams of friends share knowledge more freely, which may well accelerate learning.

Nevertheless, close friendships carry risks. When colleagues fall out, the conflict rarely stays private, and entire departments can be drawn into it. Such cases are rare, but their effects can last for years. Managers may also appear to have favoured their friends when promotions are decided, which damages trust. Avoiding such perceptions requires transparent criteria, not the suppression of friendship itself.

Organisations should therefore support friendship while setting clear boundaries. Encouraging mentoring schemes and shared projects is more effective than organising compulsory parties, since bonds that form naturally tend to last. Equally, managers should be reminded to declare close relationships when making appointments. Ultimately, the evidence suggests that friendship and professionalism are compatible. Companies that accept this, rather than discouraging informal bonds, are likely to retain talented people for longer.

1.title: Friendship and wellbeing among first-year students
1.brief: You are a member of the student services team. Write a report on a survey about friendship and loneliness among first-year students, with recommendations.
1.briefEs: Escribe un informe para servicios estudiantiles sobre una encuesta de amistad y soledad entre estudiantes de primer año.
criteria: Four headings: Introduction, Findings, Recommendations and Conclusion.
At least four phrasal verbs from the unit (hit it off, drift apart, open up, turn to).
At least two gerunds and two infinitives, including one passive gerund (being left out) in an impersonal register.
1.model:
Report: Friendship and Wellbeing among First-Year Students

Introduction
This report summarises a survey of 240 first-year students at the university, carried out in October. Its purpose is to examine how friendships formed during the first term affect wellbeing and to propose practical measures. The sample was representative of all faculties.

Findings
Most respondents reported that they had hit it off with at least one classmate within the first month. However, 38 per cent said that they had begun to drift apart from their school friends, and a quarter admitted to feeling lonely at least once a week. Students who lived in shared accommodation found it easier to open up to others, whereas commuters were more likely to turn to family for support. Several participants mentioned being left out of group chats, which they described as isolating. A minority also said that they preferred to keep their social lives separate from their studies. These figures are broadly in line with those reported in similar institutions.

Recommendations
First, the university should organise small interest-based groups during the first fortnight, since shared activities make it easier to start conversations. Second, commuter students should be offered a dedicated common room. Third, staff should encourage group chat moderators to include every member, so that nobody risks being excluded. Finally, the survey should be repeated in March to evaluate whether these measures have reduced loneliness.

Conclusion
Friendship is clearly central to student wellbeing. Modest, inexpensive measures could help newcomers settle in and reduce the risk of isolation during a difficult transition.

1.title: A buddy scheme for new employees
1.brief: Write a proposal to the human resources director for a buddy scheme that pairs new employees with experienced colleagues. Explain the problem, the scheme, its costs and its benefits.
1.briefEs: Escribe una propuesta a recursos humanos para un programa de acompañamiento que empareje a empleados nuevos con veteranos.
criteria: Headings: Background, Proposal, Costs and Expected benefits.
At least four phrasal verbs from the unit (settle in, look out for, bump into, get on with).
At least two gerunds and two infinitives, including one perfect passive form (Having been welcomed…).
1.model:
Proposal: A Buddy Scheme for New Employees

Background
Over the past year, eleven of the twenty-six people who joined our department left within six months. Exit interviews suggest that many felt isolated and struggled to settle in. Newcomers also reported that nobody had shown them how things worked.

Proposal
We propose pairing every newcomer with an experienced colleague for the first three months. The buddy would be expected to look out for the newcomer, to introduce them to the wider team and to meet them weekly for a short, informal chat. Buddies should be volunteers rather than people who have been told to take part, since genuine enthusiasm is essential. We would also organise a monthly lunch, which would give newcomers the chance to bump into colleagues from other departments and to get on with them informally. The pilot would run for six months in our department.

Costs
The scheme would cost very little. The main expense is training for buddies, a half-day workshop estimated at COP 2,400,000 for the first cohort. Time spent on weekly meetings should count as working hours. No extra staff would be required.

Expected benefits
Having been welcomed properly, newcomers are more likely to stay. We anticipate that turnover among new staff could fall by a third within a year, saving considerable recruitment costs. In addition, experienced employees would gain leadership experience, which is valuable for their own development. We would be glad to present a detailed plan at your convenience.

1.title: Volunteering to befriend: an application letter
1.brief: Write a formal letter applying to be a volunteer in a befriending programme for older people. Explain your motivation, your experience and your availability.
1.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal postulándote como voluntario en un programa de compañía para personas mayores.
criteria: At least four phrasal verbs from the unit (hit it off, strike up, let down, turn up, drop in on, keep up with).
At least two gerunds after prepositions and two infinitives.
Formal conventions: a clear purpose in the opening sentence, a polite request and the closing Yours sincerely.
1.model:
Dear Ms Quintero,

I am writing to apply for a volunteer position in your befriending programme, which I learned about through the university noticeboard.

For the past two years I have visited my neighbour, Mr Aldana, who is eighty-four and lives alone. What began as an occasional errand became a weekly routine, and we have since hit it off so well that his stories about working on the railways are now a highlight of my week. This experience has convinced me that loneliness among older people is a problem that ordinary individuals can help to solve. I would like to turn that conviction into regular, practical help.

I believe I would be well suited to the role. I am a patient listener, and I have no difficulty in striking up conversations with people I have just met. I am also reliable: I would never let a participant down by failing to turn up without notice. Should it be necessary, I am willing to drop in on people who find it hard to get out of the house, and I can keep up with the paperwork the programme requires.

I would be available on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, and I am keen to attend any training sessions you consider necessary. I have enclosed a short reference from my neighbour's daughter.

Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,
Camila Restrepo

1.title: In defence of the friend you rarely see
1.brief: Write an opinion article for a magazine arguing that friendships do not need constant contact to be real. Acknowledge the opposing view and give your reasons.
1.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de opinión defendiendo que las amistades no necesitan contacto constante para ser reales.
criteria: At least four phrasal verbs from the unit (drift apart, catch up, stand by, reach out).
At least two gerunds and two infinitives, including one perfect infinitive (to have kept up…).
A clear stance, one concession to the opposing view and a memorable final sentence.
1.model:
We are constantly told that real friendship demands constant contact. Yet some of my most valued friends are people I speak to only twice a year. I want to defend them.

Critics argue that such relationships are shallow, because friends who rarely meet are bound to drift apart. I disagree. Admittedly, I cannot pretend to have kept up with every detail of Lucía's life since she moved to Hamburg. But when we do catch up, we pick up exactly where we left off, and the conversation is anything but superficial.

What matters, in my experience, is not frequency but reliability. A friend who stands by you during a crisis, even from another continent, is worth a dozen acquaintances who comment on your photographs every day. Distance, in other words, tests friendship without necessarily damaging it. Moreover, living in an age of instant messaging, we have started to confuse visibility with closeness. Replying to a post is easy; reaching out when someone is struggling is not.

That is not to say that effort is unnecessary. Neglecting a friendship entirely will, sooner or later, lead to its disappearance. A short voice message, a birthday call or a promise to meet when you are next in town can keep the bond alive.

So let us stop feeling guilty about not being in touch more often. The best friendships are not those that never pause, but those that can pause and resume without resentment.

1.title: A farewell speech for a retiring colleague
1.brief: Write a speech to be delivered at the leaving party of a colleague who is retiring after many years. Recall how you met, praise their qualities and end with a toast.
1.briefEs: Escribe un discurso para la despedida de una colega que se jubila: cómo se conocieron, sus cualidades y un brindis final.
criteria: At least four phrasal verbs from the unit (hit it off, look up to, get through, let down, count on).
At least two gerunds and two infinitives, including one perfect infinitive (to have worked…).
A spoken register: direct address, a touch of humour and a closing toast.
1.model:
Good evening, everyone. When Gloria asked me to say a few words tonight, I agreed without thinking, which is exactly how I ended up here.

I still remember the day we met. I was twenty-three, terrified and apparently hopeless at using the photocopier. Gloria, who was already a department head, could easily have ignored me. Instead, she showed me how it worked, and we hit it off immediately. I have looked up to her ever since.

Over the years, I have seen her get through three restructurings, two floods and one unforgettable office party. I have never known her to let anyone down. She never raised her voice, yet everybody listened. When a colleague was struggling, she was the first to offer help, and when a deadline looked impossible, she was the one we could count on to find a solution.

Some people are admired for being clever. Gloria is admired for being kind, and that is much harder. I am grateful to have worked with someone who taught me that leadership means listening before deciding.

Gloria, you are retiring after thirty-one years, and I know you are looking forward to travelling at last. Please do not drift apart from us. Come back and visit, and bring photographs from every country. We will miss your laughter, your patience and, frankly, your biscuits.

So please raise your glasses. To Gloria: a wonderful colleague and an even better friend. Thank you.

2.title: Dress codes at work: necessary or outdated?
2.brief: Write a discursive essay on whether companies should still impose dress codes on their employees.
2.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo discursivo sobre si las empresas deberían seguir imponiendo códigos de vestimenta.
criteria: Two cleft sentences with what (What many managers fear is…).
Varied verb patterns (expect someone to, object to + -ing, make someone feel).
Three expressions from the unit (to dress down, to look the part, understated).
2.model:
Few workplace policies provoke as much debate as the dress code. While some organisations still require suits and ties, a growing number now allow employees to dress down every day. Which approach is more justified?

Supporters of formal dress codes argue that clothing communicates professionalism. A lawyer who turns up in trainers may struggle to look the part in front of a client, however competent she is. What many managers fear is that relaxed rules will gradually erode standards and blur the line between work and leisure. Uniforms, moreover, can create a sense of equality, preventing staff from competing over expensive brands.

Critics, however, object to being told what to wear, particularly when the rules are applied unequally. Women are frequently expected to wear heels or make-up, while men are not, and religious or cultural dress may be treated as "unprofessional". What research increasingly shows is that people who feel comfortable are more productive and more creative. Being forced into an uncomfortable suit in a city as hot as Barranquilla hardly makes anyone work better.

In my view, the most sensible solution lies somewhere in between. Rather than imposing rigid codes, companies could set broad guidelines — clean, appropriate, understated — and trust employees to adapt them to the context. A sales representative meeting a bank's directors will naturally dress differently from a programmer working remotely. What matters ultimately is not the tie, but the quality of the work.

2.title: A wardrobe that tells my story
2.brief: Write a personal article for a lifestyle magazine about one item of clothing that has special meaning for you and what it reveals about who you are.
2.briefEs: Escribe un artículo personal sobre una prenda con significado especial y lo que revela de ti.
criteria: Two or three cleft sentences with what or all (What I love about it is…).
Five different verb patterns (remind someone to, can’t help + -ing, stop + -ing / to).
Use “hand-me-downs”, “timeless” or “to pull off”.
2.model:
Most of my clothes come and go without leaving a trace. One, however, has followed me for fifteen years: a faded brown leather jacket that once belonged to my grandfather.

It came to me, like many of my childhood clothes, as a hand-me-down. My grandfather wore it on his motorbike in the 1970s, and when he stopped riding, it was hung in a wardrobe and forgotten. I found it at sixteen, put it on and refused to take it off. It was far too big, and my mother warned me that I would never pull it off. I wore it anyway.

What I love about it is not its style, although it has a timeless quality that no fast-fashion jacket could imitate. What really matters is the way it makes me feel. Whenever I wear it, I can't help remembering the stories he used to tell about crossing the Andes on that bike. It reminds me to take risks, to travel and to stay curious.

The jacket has been repaired several times. The lining has been replaced, and one sleeve bears a scar from a fall I would rather not discuss. Friends occasionally suggest I buy a new one. What they don't understand is that the wear is the whole point.

All I hope is that, one day, it will fit someone else in the family just as badly as it once fitted me.

2.title: First impressions in job interviews
2.brief: Write an article for a careers website advising young professionals on how appearance influences first impressions in interviews, and how to manage it without losing authenticity.
2.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para un portal de empleo sobre cómo la apariencia influye en la primera impresión en entrevistas.
criteria: Two cleft sentences with what and one with it (It is… that…).
A range of verb patterns (advise someone to, avoid + -ing, end up + -ing).
Use “to judge a book by its cover” and “to be dressed to the nines”.
2.model:
Dressing for Success — Without Disappearing

We are told not to judge a book by its cover, yet research suggests that interviewers form an opinion within the first seven seconds of meeting a candidate. Appearance is, inevitably, part of that impression.

What recruiters look for, above all, is appropriateness. Turning up dressed to the nines for an interview at a relaxed tech startup can be just as damaging as wearing jeans to a meeting at a law firm. It is the mismatch, rather than the clothes themselves, that sends the wrong signal: it suggests you have not done your research. Before the interview, take time to look at the company's social media and notice how employees present themselves.

Experts generally advise candidates to aim one level above the everyday dress of the workplace. If the team wears T-shirts, a smart shirt is enough; if they wear blazers, choose a suit. Avoid wearing anything you have not tried on beforehand — many people end up spending the entire interview adjusting a tight collar or uncomfortable shoes.

What is often overlooked, however, is authenticity. You do not need to erase your personality to be taken seriously. A distinctive pair of glasses or a piece of traditional jewellery can make you memorable, provided it does not distract from what you are saying.

Finally, remember that clothes open the door, but it is your preparation that keeps it open. Confidence comes from knowing your subject, not from the label on your jacket.

2.title: Uniforms and learning: what does the evidence show?
2.brief: Write an academic essay evaluating whether school uniforms improve discipline and academic results. Weigh the arguments, refer to the kind of evidence available and reach a balanced conclusion.
2.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo académico que evalúe si los uniformes escolares mejoran la disciplina y los resultados.
criteria: At least two cleft sentences (What… is…; It is… that…).
At least four different verb patterns (expect someone to, object to + -ing, make someone feel, stop + -ing).
A formal register, one expression from the unit (understated, to look the part) and a balanced conclusion.
2.model:
School uniforms are often defended as a simple way of improving discipline and results. Yet the research on this question is far less conclusive than politicians tend to suggest. This essay examines what the evidence actually shows.

Proponents expect uniforms to reduce distractions and to create a sense of belonging. What they emphasise most is equality: when everybody dresses alike, differences in family income become less visible. Some head teachers also report that uniforms help pupils look the part, behaving more seriously as a result.

However, the empirical evidence is mixed. Several large studies have found no clear link between uniforms and attainment. What the data do show is that expensive, branded uniforms place a burden on poorer families. Pupils may also object to being told what to wear, particularly when the rules make them feel uncomfortable or self-conscious.

It is not the garment that matters, but the climate of the school. A uniform that is comfortable, affordable and understated may cause no harm, whereas a rigid code enforced by punishment can damage relationships between staff and pupils. Schools should stop assuming that clothing alone changes behaviour and start investigating what actually helps children to learn.

In conclusion, uniforms are neither the solution to poor discipline nor the threat to freedom that critics describe. Their value depends on cost, comfort and the way they are introduced. Policy should therefore rest on local evidence rather than on nostalgia.

2.title: Staff appearance and guest satisfaction at a hotel
2.brief: You are an assistant manager at a hotel. Write a report on how the appearance of front-desk staff affects guest satisfaction, based on a questionnaire, with recommendations.
2.briefEs: Escribe un informe para la gerencia de un hotel sobre cómo la apariencia del personal de recepción afecta la satisfacción de los huéspedes.
criteria: Headings: Introduction, Findings, Recommendations and Conclusion.
At least two cleft sentences (What… was…; It is… that…).
At least four verb patterns (expect someone to, object to + -ing, make someone feel, insist on + -ing) and one expression from the unit (dress down, understated).
2.model:
Report: Staff Appearance and Guest Satisfaction at the Hotel Mirador

Introduction
This report examines whether the appearance of front-desk staff influences guest satisfaction at the Hotel Mirador. It is based on 150 guest questionnaires and observations carried out over two weeks. The aim is to identify practical improvements.

Findings
Guests generally expect receptionists to look professional, and 82 per cent rated the current uniform as satisfactory. Overall satisfaction with the front desk was 4.3 out of 5. What they criticised most was the condition of the garments rather than the style. Several respondents objected to seeing stained or creased jackets, which made them feel that standards were slipping. It is the evening team that attracts most complaints, probably because their uniforms are washed less often. Interestingly, guests did not mind staff dressing down on Fridays, provided that the clothes were clean and understated.

Recommendations
We recommend replacing the evening uniforms, which are now more than four years old, and allowing staff to exchange them whenever they show signs of wear. Managers should insist on checking appearance at the start of every shift, but they should also remember to thank staff who maintain high standards. A relaxed Friday policy could be introduced on a trial basis for three months.

Conclusion
Guests care less about fashion than about neatness. What the hotel needs is not a new design, but a consistent standard of care. These modest changes would cost little and would reinforce the impression of professionalism that the management wishes to project.

2.title: Clothes swap day for our school
2.brief: Write a proposal to the head teacher for a clothes swap day at your school. Explain the aim, the organisation, the cost and the expected results.
2.briefEs: Escribe una propuesta a la directora para organizar un día de intercambio de ropa en tu colegio.
criteria: Headings: Aim, Organisation, Budget and Expected outcomes.
At least two cleft sentences (What we hope to achieve is…; It is… who…).
At least four verb patterns (ask someone to, expect someone to, stop + -ing, suggest + -ing) and one expression from the unit (hand-me-down, timeless, pull off).
2.model:
Proposal: Clothes Swap Day at Colegio San Martín

Aim
We propose organising a clothes swap day, at which students bring items they no longer wear and exchange them for others. Many of us own clothes that we rarely wear, while others cannot afford new ones. What we hope to achieve is a more sustainable attitude to clothing, as well as some fun.

Organisation
The event would take place in the school hall on a Friday afternoon. Each participant would receive a token for every garment donated, and tokens could then be exchanged for other items. We would ask students to bring only clean, good-quality clothes, and volunteers would sort them by size. Items that nobody takes would be donated to a local charity. It is the older students who could help most, by advising younger ones on how to pull off a style that looks timeless rather than fashionable for a single season.

Budget
The cost would be minimal. Posters and clothes rails amount to approximately COP 350,000, which the student council has agreed to cover. Teachers have kindly offered to lend the hall free of charge.

Expected outcomes
We expect at least eighty students to take part and several hundred garments to find a second life. Many pupils already wear hand-me-downs from siblings, so the idea will not seem strange. Local newspapers may also cover the day, which would raise the school's profile. What matters most is that students stop thinking of clothes as disposable. We suggest repeating the event each term.

2.title: Review: an exhibition on everyday clothing
2.brief: Write a critical review of an exhibition, real or imagined, about the history of clothing. Describe it, evaluate its strengths and weaknesses and say whether you would recommend it.
2.briefEs: Escribe una reseña crítica de una exposición, real o imaginada, sobre la historia de la ropa: descripción, fortalezas, debilidades y recomendación.
criteria: At least two cleft sentences (What impresses most is…; It is… that…).
At least three verb patterns (want someone to, make someone feel, expect someone to, encourage someone to) and one expression from the unit (timeless, understated, hand-me-down).
Balanced evaluation: at least one strength, one weakness and a final rating.
2.model:
Threads of Time: a thoughtful but uneven exhibition

The museum's new exhibition, Threads of Time, traces the history of everyday clothing in Colombia from the 1920s to the present. Over four rooms, it combines original garments, photographs and oral histories. Its curators clearly want visitors to see garments as historical documents rather than mere fashion.

What impresses most is the quality of the objects. A farmer's woollen ruana, a pair of 1970s flared trousers and a timeless black dress worn by a famous singer are displayed with short texts that make visitors feel connected to the people who wore them. The section on hand-me-downs, built around letters between sisters, is particularly moving.

Unfortunately, the exhibition is less successful in its final rooms. All the information about recent fast fashion is presented on screens, and it is hard to read the captions in the dim light. It is the lack of critical perspective that disappoints most: the curators seem reluctant to discuss working conditions in the industry, which many visitors would expect them to address.

Even so, these weaknesses should not stop anyone from going. The exhibition's design is understated, allowing the clothes to speak for themselves, and the guided tours, led by retired seamstresses, are a delight. I would encourage visitors to book one in advance. The museum is easy to reach by metro, and entry is free on Sundays. Threads of Time is not a perfect show, but it is a memorable and surprisingly personal one. Three stars out of four.

2.title: Complaint about an online order
2.brief: Write a formal letter of complaint to an online clothing retailer about an order that arrived wrong and damaged. Explain what happened and state what you expect the company to do.
2.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal de reclamo a una tienda de ropa en línea por un pedido que llegó equivocado y dañado.
criteria: At least one cleft sentence (What arrived was…; It is not only… that…).
At least four verb patterns (be told to, expect someone to, remember + -ing, arrange for something to be…).
Formal conventions: Dear Sir or Madam, a clear request with a deadline, Yours faithfully; no contractions.
2.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about an order I placed on 3 October, which was delivered last week in unsatisfactory condition. I have been a customer for three years and have never before had cause for complaint. I had ordered a navy wool coat, advertised on your website as "timeless and understated".

What arrived was a thin synthetic jacket in a different shade, with a broken zip. I contacted your customer service team on 14 October, and was told to wait five working days for a reply. I am still waiting. It is not only the error that concerns me but also the lack of communication that followed. I do not expect a company of your reputation to leave customers feeling ignored.

I therefore request a full refund of 389,000 Colombian pesos, including the delivery charge. I would also be grateful if you could arrange for the jacket to be collected from my address, as I have no wish to return it at my own expense. Should I not receive a satisfactory reply within ten days, I shall have no alternative but to contact the consumer protection authority.

I have attached the order confirmation, photographs of the item and a copy of my correspondence with your team. I remember being assured, when I placed the order, that returns would be free and refunds processed within a week. I trust that you will honour that promise.

I look forward to your prompt response.

Yours faithfully,
Andrea Villamizar

2.title: Opening speech for a second-hand fashion show
2.brief: Write the opening speech for a charity fashion show in which all the clothes come from second-hand shops. Welcome the audience, explain the idea and persuade them to value second-hand clothing.
2.briefEs: Escribe el discurso de apertura de un desfile benéfico con ropa de segunda mano: da la bienvenida, explica la idea y persuade al público.
criteria: At least two cleft sentences (What I want you to remember is…; It is… that…).
At least four verb patterns (want someone to, ask someone to, persuade someone to, stop + -ing, help someone + base form).
A spoken register with direct address, a touch of humour and at least two expressions from the unit (dressed to the nines, to pull off).
2.model:
Good evening, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to our second Second Chance Fashion Show.

Look around you. Many of you are dressed to the nines tonight, and I have a confession to make: almost everything you are wearing came from our charity shop. That sequinned jacket? Four pounds. Those leather shoes? A gift from a neighbour. And the gentleman at the front who looks as though he has stepped off a catwalk is, in fact, my uncle, in a suit that once belonged to my grandfather.

What I want you to remember tonight is that style does not depend on money. It is imagination that makes an outfit memorable. Anyone can wear an expensive label, but it takes confidence to pull off a vintage coat with trainers, and that is exactly what our models will show you.

I also ask you to think about where clothes end up. We throw away millions of garments every year, and most could be worn again. We would like to persuade you to stop seeing second-hand clothing as embarrassing and to start seeing it as smart.

Every ticket you bought tonight will help us provide winter coats for children in our community. Last year, you helped us dress forty-two children, and I hope we can beat that record tonight. 3.title: Should AI be used to mark students' work?
3.brief: Write a discursive essay on whether artificial intelligence should be used to grade essays and exams in schools and universities.
3.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo discursivo sobre si la inteligencia artificial debería usarse para calificar exámenes y ensayos.
criteria: Accurate use of articles (a / the / zero article) with abstract and specific nouns.
Three -ing clauses (Having analysed…, Using algorithms, …).
Four expressions from the unit (cutting-edge, drawback, unintended consequences, to roll out).
3.model:
In recent years, a number of universities have begun to roll out software that uses artificial intelligence to grade students' work. Supporters describe it as a game-changer; critics see it as a threat to education itself.

The advantages are considerable. Marking hundreds of essays is exhausting, and tired teachers are not always consistent. Using cutting-edge language models, a computer can assess grammar, structure and argument in seconds, providing instant feedback that students can act on immediately. Freed from repetitive grading, teachers would have more time for the human side of teaching: explaining, motivating and listening.

However, the drawbacks are equally serious. Algorithms are trained on existing data, which means they may reward conventional writing and penalise originality. Having been designed mainly in English-speaking countries, many systems also struggle with the varieties of English used by students in Latin America or Asia. Perhaps the greatest danger lies in the unintended consequences: if students know that a machine is reading their work, they may simply learn to write for the machine, producing formulaic texts that tick the right boxes.

Weighing up these arguments, I believe that AI should play a supporting role rather than a decisive one. It can be a valuable tool for checking drafts and spotting errors, but the final grade — and the judgement about what makes an idea genuinely interesting — should remain in human hands. Education is, after all, a relationship between people, not merely the processing of data.

3.title: A report on technology use at work
3.brief: Your manager has asked you to write a report on how a new piece of technology (a chatbot, a project-management app, video conferencing) has affected your team, with recommendations.
3.briefEs: Escribe un informe para tu jefe sobre el impacto de una nueva tecnología en tu equipo, con recomendaciones.
criteria: Headings and an impersonal, formal register.
Three -ing clauses for concision (Comparing the figures, …).
Correct articles with general vs specific references (the software, technology in general).
3.model:
Report: Impact of the Customer-Service Chatbot

Introduction
This report evaluates the chatbot introduced in our customer-service department in March and makes recommendations for its future use. It is based on usage data and interviews with twelve members of staff.

Findings
Comparing the figures for the first and second quarters, the average waiting time for customers fell from eleven minutes to three. The chatbot now resolves approximately 40% of enquiries without human intervention, mostly simple requests such as changing passwords or checking the status of an order.

However, several problems were identified. Having been trained on generic data, the software frequently misunderstands regional expressions, which has led to a number of frustrated customers. Staff also reported that complaints transferred from the chatbot tend to be more complex and emotionally charged, increasing pressure on the team. Two employees described feeling that their role had become "damage control".

Recommendations
• The chatbot should be retrained using transcripts of real conversations with Colombian customers.
• Customers should be offered the option of speaking to a person at any stage, rather than only after three failed attempts.
• Training in handling difficult calls should be provided for all agents.
• The system's performance should be reviewed again in six months.

Conclusion
Overall, the technology has delivered clear gains in efficiency. Nevertheless, unless the issues outlined above are addressed, there is a risk that customer satisfaction and staff morale will decline.

3.title: The invention that changed my family's life
3.brief: Write an article for a science magazine's readers' section about a technology (old or new) that transformed your family's daily life.
3.briefEs: Escribe un artículo para la sección de lectores de una revista científica sobre una tecnología que transformó la vida de tu familia.
criteria: Precise use of the definite article for inventions and institutions (the washing machine, the internet).
Three -ing clauses, including one perfect (Having lived…).
Use “breakthrough”, “obsolete” and “to render obsolete”.
3.model:
When people talk about technological breakthroughs, they usually mention the internet or the smartphone. For my family, the revolution was far humbler: a solar panel.

My grandparents live on a small farm in the mountains of Cauca, two hours from the nearest town. Having lived without a reliable electricity supply for most of their lives, they organised their days around the sun. Cooking was done with firewood, homework was done before dark, and the only radio ran on batteries that were expensive and hard to find.

In 2017, a government programme installed a set of solar panels on their roof. The change was immediate. Using a single panel and a battery, they could suddenly light the house, charge a phone and run a small fridge. My grandmother began selling cheese and milk to neighbours, keeping them cool for the first time. My younger cousins, studying by electric light, saw their grades improve.

The panels did not render the old ways obsolete overnight. My grandfather still prefers to cook on the wood stove, insisting that the food tastes better. Yet the technology has transformed what is possible in a place the national grid has never reached.

What strikes me most is how little attention such innovations receive. We celebrate the latest phone, but for millions of rural families, the real game-changer is the ability to switch on a light.

3.title: Is the digital divide still widening?
3.brief: Write an academic essay on whether technology is narrowing or widening the gap between people who have good digital access and those who do not. Consider access, skills and public policy.
3.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo académico sobre si la tecnología reduce o amplía la brecha entre quienes tienen buen acceso digital y quienes no.
criteria: Accurate use of articles with generic and specific nouns (technology, the internet, a laptop).
At least three -ing clauses (Having installed…, Libraries offering…, Ignoring…).
At least four expressions from the unit (cutting-edge, roll out, game-changer, unintended consequences).
3.model:
The internet is often described as the great equaliser. Yet millions of people still lack a reliable connection, and the gap between those with access to technology and those without it may be widening rather than narrowing. This essay examines why.

Access is only the first obstacle. Having installed fibre-optic cables in cities, many governments consider the problem solved, but rural households often face prices they cannot afford. A smartphone with a limited data plan is not the same as a laptop with a stable connection, and students who rely on the former are at a clear disadvantage. Moreover, cutting-edge services such as online banking or telemedicine are designed for users with fast connections and recent devices.

A second, less visible problem is skills. Knowing how to use technology safely is a form of literacy, and older adults, in particular, may be excluded from services that are rolled out without adequate training. Libraries offering free courses have proved effective in several countries, although such programmes rarely receive stable funding.

Admittedly, technology can also reduce inequality. Free educational platforms are a genuine game-changer, since they allow a teenager in a remote village to follow the same lessons as a student in a capital city. However, the benefits reach only those who are already connected. Unless governments treat internet access as an essential service, like water or electricity, the unintended consequences of rapid digitalisation will fall hardest on the people least able to bear them. Ignoring that reality, we risk building a digital society for the few, not the many.

3.title: Executive summary: a telemedicine pilot
3.brief: Write the executive summary of a report on a telemedicine pilot in rural clinics. State the purpose, the key findings, a recommendation and the next steps for busy decision-makers.
3.briefEs: Escribe el resumen ejecutivo de un informe sobre un piloto de telemedicina en clínicas rurales para quienes toman decisiones.
criteria: Headings: Purpose, Key findings, Recommendation and Next steps.
At least three -ing clauses (Using…, Having analysed…, forcing…).
At least three expressions from the unit (drawback, roll out, unintended consequences) and correct articles with specific references (the platform, the regional hospital).
3.model:
Executive Summary: Telemedicine Pilot in Rural Clinics

Purpose
This summary presents the results of a six-month pilot in which a telemedicine service was introduced in four rural clinics in the department of Boyacá. The pilot sought to determine whether the technology could reduce the need for patients to travel to the regional hospital.

Key findings
Using video consultations, nurses were able to consult specialists in real time, and 62 per cent of cases were resolved locally. Patients saved an average of five hours of travel, and satisfaction was high. Having analysed the records, the evaluation team also found that waiting times for specialist appointments fell from forty days to twelve. The main drawback was connectivity: in one clinic, calls dropped during bad weather, forcing staff to reschedule appointments by telephone.

Recommendation
We recommend rolling out the service to a further twelve clinics over the next two years, starting with those that already have a stable connection. Before the launch, the health department should invest in satellite equipment for remote sites and train staff in the use of the platform. Doing so would cost approximately COP 900 million, a modest sum compared with the cost of transporting patients by ambulance.

Next steps
If the board approves the plan in March, the first new clinics could begin operating by September. A final evaluation should be published after the first full year, so that the unintended consequences of the expansion, such as pressure on specialist doctors, can be identified early.

3.briefEs: Escribe una propuesta al comité de sostenibilidad de tu universidad para recoger y reciclar aparatos electrónicos viejos.

Proposal: An Electronic Waste Collection Point on Campus

Background
Every year, students and staff discard hundreds of old phones, chargers and laptops, most of which end up in ordinary bins. Electronic waste contains valuable metals as well as toxic substances, so disposing of it carelessly harms both the environment and the economy. Our campus currently has no system for dealing with it.

Proposal
We propose installing three secure collection points, one in the library, one in the engineering building and one in the main cafeteria. Having registered with an authorised recycling company, the university would arrange for the equipment to be collected every month. Devices that still work would be repaired by students from the electronics course, then donated to schools. Those that are obsolete would be dismantled and recycled.

Costs
The main costs are the three containers, priced at COP 1,200,000 each, and a publicity campaign costing about COP 800,000. The recycling company would collect the equipment free of charge in exchange for the materials.

Expected outcomes
Using the first semester as a trial, we expect to collect at least one tonne of electronic waste. This would be a small breakthrough for a university of our size, but the greater value lies in changing habits. Students who see the containers every day are more likely to think twice before throwing away a broken phone. Success will be measured by weight collected, number of devices repaired and responses to a short survey. We would welcome the opportunity to discuss the proposal with the committee.

3.title: Review: a documentary on algorithms
3.brief: Write a critical review of a documentary, real or imagined, about how algorithms influence our lives. Evaluate its strengths and weaknesses and give a recommendation and rating.
3.briefEs: Escribe una reseña crítica de un documental, real o imaginado, sobre cómo los algoritmos influyen en nuestras vidas.
criteria: At least three -ing clauses (recording…, Rather than using…, Having raised…).
At least three expressions from the unit (unintended consequences, cutting-edge, game-changer) and accurate articles.
Balanced evaluation with at least one strength, one weakness and a final rating.
3.model:
The Quiet Machine: a documentary that asks the right questions

The Quiet Machine, a new documentary now streaming, investigates how recommendation algorithms shape what we watch, buy and believe. Directed by Marta Liendo, it follows three families over a year, recording how their daily routines are influenced by the software on their phones. Running for ninety-four minutes, it is both a family portrait and an investigation.

Its greatest strength is its restraint. Rather than using dramatic music or alarming statistics, Liendo lets the families speak. A teenager admits that she no longer chooses songs herself, while a retired teacher describes how a video platform gradually led him towards increasingly extreme opinions. These moments illustrate the unintended consequences of cutting-edge technology far more effectively than any expert could. The cinematography, too, is notably intimate.

Unfortunately, the film is less convincing when it turns to solutions. Having raised serious questions about privacy, it offers little more than a vague call for regulation, and the brief interviews with engineers feel rushed. A discussion of how other countries have responded would have been a welcome addition. The pace also slows noticeably in the middle, where several scenes repeat the same point.

Nevertheless, this is an intelligent and humane film. It will not be a game-changer for the debate on technology, but it may well change how its viewers use their phones tonight. Anyone worried about the effect of the internet on young people should watch it, preferably together with them. Four stars out of five.

3.title: Why the right to repair matters
3.brief: Write an opinion article for a newspaper arguing that consumers should have the right to repair the devices they buy. Use a personal example, acknowledge the drawbacks and propose action.
3.briefEs: Escribe un artículo de opinión defendiendo que los consumidores tengan derecho a reparar los aparatos que compran.
criteria: At least three -ing clauses (using glue…, Requiring companies…, buying…).
At least three expressions from the unit (render obsolete, drawback, unintended consequences, breakthrough).
Accurate use of articles, a personal opening and a closing sentence that leaves the reader with a question or call to action.
3.model:
My washing machine broke last month. The technician told me that the part I needed was no longer manufactured, and that a new machine would cost less than the repair. I bought a new one, and I have been feeling uneasy ever since.

My experience is far from unusual. Manufacturers increasingly design products that are difficult to open, using glue instead of screws and refusing to sell spare parts. Software updates can render a perfectly good phone obsolete within a few years. Each of these decisions may look sensible to an accountant, but together they produce enormous quantities of waste.

That is why the so-called right to repair matters. Requiring companies to supply parts and manuals would allow independent technicians to fix devices at a reasonable price. Several countries have already passed laws along these lines, and early results are encouraging. Admittedly, there are drawbacks: some products would become slightly more expensive, and safety standards would need careful supervision. Even so, the unintended consequences of the current system, from mountains of discarded electronics to the loss of local repair skills, are far more worrying.

Repairing something is also a small act of independence. We are told that the latest model is always a breakthrough, yet the real innovation may lie in making things last. I would rather own a machine that can be mended than one that is merely new. Next time something of mine breaks, I intend to ask one question before buying a replacement: can it be fixed?

4.title: Why do intelligent people believe in superstitions?
4.brief: Write a discursive essay exploring why superstitions persist in modern, educated societies, and whether they do any harm.
4.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo discursivo sobre por qué persisten las supersticiones en sociedades modernas y si hacen daño.
criteria: Four reporting verbs with that-clauses or infinitives (claim, argue, suggest, maintain).
Two passive reporting structures (It is believed that…, X is said to…).
Use “anecdotal”, “to debunk” and “to lend credence to”.
4.model:
In an age of space exploration and genetic engineering, it might seem surprising that millions of people still avoid walking under ladders or refuse to fly on Friday the 13th. Yet superstitions remain remarkably persistent, even among the highly educated.

Psychologists suggest that superstitions offer a sense of control in situations that are inherently uncertain. Athletes are known to follow elaborate rituals before competitions; tennis star Rafael Nadal, for instance, is said to arrange his water bottles in exactly the same position at every match. It is widely believed that such routines reduce anxiety, which may in turn improve performance — lending credence, ironically, to the idea that the ritual "works".

Others argue that superstitions are simply cultural habits passed down through generations. In Colombia, many families still burn sage on New Year's Eve or walk around the block with a suitcase to guarantee travel. Few genuinely believe in these customs, but they maintain that abandoning them would feel like breaking a link with their grandparents.

Most superstitions are harmless, and some may even be beneficial. However, problems arise when people base serious decisions on anecdotal evidence. Rejecting medical treatment in favour of a lucky charm, or refusing to vaccinate a child because of an omen, can have tragic consequences. Scientists have debunked countless such beliefs, but debunking alone rarely changes behaviour.

Ultimately, superstition seems to be part of human nature. The challenge is not to eliminate it, but to ensure it never takes the place of reason.

4.title: A report on a viral claim
4.brief: Write a fact-checking report for a news website on a viral claim (a miracle cure, a conspiracy theory, a fake celebrity quote). Report what was claimed, by whom, and what the evidence shows.
4.briefEs: Escribe un informe de verificación de datos sobre una afirmación viral: qué se dijo, quién lo dijo y qué muestran las pruebas.
criteria: Five different reporting verbs (claim, allege, deny, insist, acknowledge).
Three passive reporting clauses (It has been suggested that…, is thought to have…).
An objective, neutral register.
4.model:
FACT CHECK: Does Lemon Water Cure Diabetes?

A video claiming that drinking hot lemon water every morning can cure type 2 diabetes has been shared more than three million times on social media in the past week.

The claim
In the video, a man who describes himself as a "natural health expert" alleges that he cured his own diabetes in thirty days by drinking lemon water and avoiding all medication. He insists that doctors hide this "secret" because pharmaceutical companies would lose money. The video is thought to have originated on a Brazilian channel before being translated into Spanish.

What the evidence shows
We consulted three endocrinologists and reviewed the scientific literature. While lemon juice is a healthy drink, there is no evidence that it can cure diabetes. It has been suggested in some small studies that citrus fruits may slightly reduce blood sugar spikes after meals, but researchers acknowledge that these effects are minimal. Dr. Ana Lucía Barrios of the Colombian Diabetes Association warned that patients who stop taking their medication risk serious complications, including kidney failure and blindness.

When contacted, the author of the video denied that he was giving medical advice, claiming that he was simply "sharing his experience". The account has since been removed by the platform.

Verdict: FALSE
Lemon water is not a cure for diabetes. Patients should never stop prescribed treatment without consulting a doctor.

4.title: Lucky charms and rituals
4.brief: Write a blog post about the superstitions and rituals in your family or region. Report what people say about them and reflect on why you keep (or reject) them.
4.briefEs: Escribe una entrada de blog sobre las supersticiones de tu familia o región y reflexiona por qué las mantienes o rechazas.
criteria: Reporting verbs with different patterns (warn someone not to, swear that, be supposed to).
Two passive reporting structures (is believed to, is said to bring).
Use “far-fetched”, “gullible”, “to take something at face value”.
4.model:
My Grandmother's Rules for a Lucky Life

Growing up in Popayán, I learned that luck was something you had to work for — or at least something you could protect through a long list of rules, mostly invented by my grandmother.

She warned us never to put a handbag on the floor, because doing so is believed to make your money "run away". She swore that a black butterfly in the house announced bad news, and that if your left hand itched, you were about to receive money. On New Year's Eve, we were supposed to eat twelve grapes at midnight, one for each wish, and wear yellow underwear for good fortune. A sábila (aloe vera) plant hung behind the front door is said to keep envy away; we had three.

As a teenager, I found all this far-fetched. I accused my family of being gullible and refused to eat the grapes, which my grandmother took as a personal insult. These days, my attitude has softened. I don't take any of these beliefs at face value, but I have started to see them as a kind of family language — a way of expressing hope and fear without having to name them.

So yes, I still hang a sábila behind my door. I don't think it protects me from envy. But every time I see it, I think of her, and that feels like a kind of luck in itself.

4.title: Why do conspiracy theories spread in a crisis?
4.brief: Write an academic essay explaining why conspiracy theories multiply in times of crisis and what could be done to limit their influence.
4.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo académico que explique por qué se multiplican las teorías de conspiración en las crisis y cómo limitar su influencia.
criteria: At least four reporting verbs with that-clauses or infinitives (claim, insist, suggest, argue, maintain, deny + -ing).
At least two passive reporting structures (It is argued that…, X are said to…, X are believed to…).
At least three expressions from the unit (far-fetched, to debunk, anecdotal, to take at face value).
4.model:
Whenever a society faces a crisis, conspiracy theories seem to multiply. During the pandemic, for example, it was widely claimed that the virus had been created deliberately, and some people insisted that vaccines contained tracking devices. Why do such far-fetched ideas find so many believers? This essay explores the causes and considers what can be done.

Psychologists suggest that uncertainty is the main driver. When events are frightening and complex, a simple story with a clear culprit is more comforting than the messy truth. It is often argued that conspiracy theories offer a sense of control, and they are said to be especially attractive to people who feel powerless. Social media amplifies the effect: algorithms are believed to reward emotional content, so that the most alarming claims travel fastest.

Debunking these theories is harder than it seems. Believers frequently deny having been misled, and they maintain that official sources have an interest in hiding the truth. Presenting more facts can even backfire, because people tend to defend their existing views more strongly when challenged. Anecdotal evidence, such as a friend's story, often carries more weight than a scientific study.

A more promising approach, it seems, is prevention rather than correction. Schools that teach pupils to check sources and to question headlines are reported to produce more sceptical readers. Ultimately, the best protection against conspiracy theories is not ridicule but trust: people who feel heard by institutions are less likely to take wild claims at face value.

4.title: Report: how teenagers verify information online
4.brief: Write a report on a survey of secondary pupils about how they check information they find online. Present the findings in a neutral tone and make recommendations.
4.briefEs: Escribe un informe sobre una encuesta a estudiantes de secundaria acerca de cómo verifican la información en línea.
criteria: Headings: Introduction, Findings, Recommendations and Conclusion.
At least four different reporting verbs (claim, admit, insist, warn, suggest).
At least two passive reporting structures (It is thought that…, It is believed that…) and a neutral, objective register with the word “hoax”.
4.model:
Report: How Teenagers Verify Information Online

Introduction
This report presents the findings of a survey of 180 pupils aged fifteen to seventeen at a secondary school in Cali. The sample included pupils from all four year groups. The survey asked how they decide whether information found online can be trusted. The results were collected anonymously in March.

Findings
Most pupils claimed that they always check the source of a story before sharing it. However, interviews suggest that this is not the case in practice. Only a quarter admitted to having shared a post without reading it, but classroom observations indicate that the figure is considerably higher. One pupil insisted that she could recognise false news by its tone, whereas teachers warned that sophisticated hoaxes are designed to sound reliable. It is thought that pupils tend to trust content shared by friends, regardless of its origin. Moreover, few respondents were aware that an image can be altered or taken out of context.

Recommendations
The school is advised to include source-checking in the curriculum, starting with practical exercises on reverse image searches. Teachers should warn pupils not to treat popularity as evidence of accuracy. It is also recommended that the exercise be repeated annually so that progress can be measured.

Conclusion
Pupils are confident about their ability to detect false information, but there is little evidence that this confidence is justified. It is believed that structured training would reduce the number of hoaxes shared within the school, although further research is needed.

4.title: Media literacy workshops for older adults
4.brief: Write a proposal to a public library for a series of workshops that teach older adults to recognise false information on messaging apps. Explain the problem, the plan, the budget and the expected results.
4.briefEs: Escribe una propuesta a una biblioteca pública para talleres que enseñen a adultos mayores a reconocer información falsa en aplicaciones de mensajería.
criteria: Headings: Background, Proposal, Budget and Expected outcomes.
At least four reporting verbs (report, admit, insist, suggest, encourage someone to…).
At least two passive reporting structures (are believed to…, are said to…) and two expressions from the unit (gullible, hoax, anecdotal).
4.model:
Proposal: Media Literacy Workshops for Older Adults

Background
Library staff report that many older users receive chain messages on their phones containing false health advice, and some admit to having forwarded them to relatives. Such messages are believed to spread fastest on messaging apps, and they are said to be most persuasive when they appear to come from a family member. An informal poll of our users found that one in three over-sixties had forwarded at least one hoax in the previous month. These users are not gullible; they simply lack the tools to check what they read.

Proposal
We propose a series of six free workshops, held monthly at the central library. Each session would last ninety minutes and would be led by a volunteer journalist. Participants would learn to recognise warning signs, such as alarming headlines and missing sources, and to use free fact-checking websites. We would encourage them to bring messages they have received, so that the group can examine them together. Facilitators would insist on a respectful atmosphere, since nobody should feel embarrassed about having been misled.

Budget
The programme would cost approximately COP 3,000,000 in total, covering materials, refreshments and a small fee for the journalist. The library has agreed to provide the room free of charge.

Expected outcomes
Participants are expected to become more confident in checking information, and they are likely to pass these skills on to their families. We will ask them to complete a short questionnaire before and after the course, so that any change can be measured. Anecdotal feedback from similar projects suggests that people who attend such workshops are far less likely to share unverified messages.

4.title: Review: a podcast on urban legends
4.brief: Write a critical review of a podcast, real or imagined, that investigates rumours and urban legends. Evaluate its method, its strengths and its weaknesses, and say who should listen.
4.briefEs: Escribe una reseña crítica de un pódcast, real o imaginado, que investigue rumores y leyendas urbanas.
criteria: Reporting language in at least four places (claim, deny, admit, suggest, remind someone that…).
At least two passive reporting structures (is said to have…, is thought to have…).
At least two expressions from the unit (to debunk, anecdotal, to take at face value) and a balanced evaluation with a final rating.
4.model:
Half True: a podcast that debunks with a smile

Half True, a weekly podcast presented by journalist Camilo Duarte, examines urban legends and viral rumours, from haunted hospitals to miracle diets. Each episode of about thirty minutes traces a single story back to its origins.

The format is simple but effective. Duarte begins by reporting what is claimed, then interviews the people who first spread the story, and finally consults an expert. In one memorable episode, a famous legend about a ghost in a Medellín school is said to have started as a prank by two pupils in the 1980s. They admitted that they had never expected anyone to believe it, which is both funny and revealing.

Where the podcast falls short is in its treatment of sources. Several episodes rely on anecdotal evidence, and guests are occasionally allowed to claim almost anything without challenge. Sometimes the evidence is simply asserted rather than shown. A programme devoted to debunking should be more careful. The humour, too, can become repetitive, especially when Duarte denies being tempted by the very beliefs he mocks.

These flaws aside, Half True deserves its growing audience. It treats believers with respect rather than contempt, and it reminds us that nobody is immune to a good story. Listeners who are tempted to take rumours at face value will find it a useful and entertaining corrective. It is thought to have more than fifty thousand regular listeners, which is impressive for an independent production. Four stars out of five.

4.title: A request for a correction
4.brief: Write a formal letter to a newspaper editor requesting a correction to an article that contained inaccurate claims about your organisation. Set the record straight and say what you want the newspaper to do.
4.briefEs: Escribe una carta formal al director de un periódico pidiendo la rectificación de un artículo con afirmaciones inexactas sobre tu organización.
criteria: Formal letter conventions: Dear Editor, a clear purpose in the first sentence, a precise request and Yours faithfully.
At least four reporting verbs or structures (state, deny, insist, urge someone to, be told that).
At least two passive reporting structures (is believed to have…, are said to have been…) and the expression “to lend credence to”.
4.model:
Dear Editor,

I am writing to request a correction to the article "Local Clinic Accused of Negligence", published in your edition of 12 March. The article states that the clinic is believed to have ignored three official warnings, and that its director denied the allegations only after being contacted by journalists. Both claims are inaccurate.

As the director of the clinic, I wish to set the record straight. First, the warnings mentioned in your article are said to have been issued last year. In fact, only one inspection report was received, and the deficiencies it identified were corrected within two weeks. I can provide the relevant documents. Second, I issued a statement before any journalist contacted me, and I insisted from the outset that an independent inquiry should be held. I have also repeatedly invited the authorities to carry one out.

I am aware that your reporter was told by an anonymous source that patients had been put at risk. I would urge you to treat such claims with caution. Unverified rumours of this kind can seriously damage the reputation of a health centre on which hundreds of families depend, and they lend credence to fears that have no basis in fact.

I would therefore be grateful if you would publish a correction in the same section of the newspaper, together with the brief statement attached to this letter. I would also welcome the opportunity to meet your editorial team to discuss how future coverage might be handled.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Yours faithfully,
Dr Sandra Pineda
Director, Clínica San Rafael

4.title: Check first, share second
4.brief: Write a speech for a school assembly persuading classmates to check information before sharing it. Begin with a short story, explain why false news works and give three practical pieces of advice.
4.briefEs: Escribe un discurso para una asamblea escolar que convenza a tus compañeros de verificar antes de compartir. Empieza con una anécdota y da tres consejos.
criteria: At least four reporting verbs (claim, admit, warn, say, ask).
At least two passive reporting structures (It was said to have…, It is often said that…).
At least three expressions from the unit (hoax, gullible, to take at face value, far-fetched) and a spoken register with direct address.
4.model:
Good morning, everyone. Let me begin with a story. Last year, a message went round our class chat claiming that school would close for a week because of a mysterious strike. It was said to have come from the head teacher's office. Within an hour, half the school was celebrating.

The message was a hoax. Nobody had called a strike. The sender later admitted to having invented it as a joke, and, to be fair, it was a very convincing one. But it taught me something important: none of us is as sceptical as we like to think.

It is often said that only gullible people believe false news. I do not agree. Clever, careful people are fooled every day, because false stories are designed to be believed. They are written to make us angry or afraid, and when we are angry or afraid, we stop asking questions.

So I would like to ask you to do three things. First, never take a headline at face value. Second, ask who is claiming this, and what they gain from it. Third, if a story sounds too far-fetched to be true, it probably is, so wait before you share it.

Researchers warn that false stories often spread faster than the corrections that follow them, and I believe it. That is why we, the readers, must be the filter.

Let us be the school that checks first and shares second. Thank you.

5.title: Has streaming killed the cinema?
5.brief: Write a discursive essay on whether streaming platforms are destroying the cinema-going experience or giving it new life.
5.briefEs: Escribe un ensayo discursivo sobre si las plataformas de streaming están destruyendo el cine o dándole nueva vida.
criteria: Four sentence adverbs (admittedly, arguably, undeniably, ultimately).
Two “such…that” or “so…that” structures.
Use “blockbuster”, “to binge-watch” and “critically acclaimed”.
5.model:
When the first streaming platforms appeared, few people imagined that they would one day release more films than Hollywood's traditional studios. Today, the question is no longer whether streaming will change cinema, but whether cinemas themselves will survive.

Undeniably, the convenience of streaming has transformed viewing habits. Audiences can binge-watch an entire series in a weekend without leaving the sofa, and the cost of a monthly subscription is lower than that of two cinema tickets. The pandemic accelerated this trend so dramatically that many cinemas never reopened. Arguably, platforms have also democratised filmmaking: directors from Colombia, Nigeria or Korea now reach global audiences that would have been unthinkable twenty years ago.

Admittedly, something is lost along the way. Watching a film on a phone, interrupted by notifications, is hardly the experience its creators intended. The collective emotion of a full cinema — laughing, gasping, crying together — cannot be reproduced at home. Moreover, algorithms tend to promote content similar to what we have already seen, so that risky, original projects struggle to find funding.

Yet cinemas are not dead. Big-screen blockbusters still break box-office records, and many critically acclaimed films owe their success to a theatrical release that generates conversation. Some cinemas have reinvented themselves with such comfortable seats and such carefully curated programmes that going out has become an event once again.

Ultimately, streaming and cinema seem destined to coexist, each offering something the other cannot.

5.title: A TV series pitch
5.brief: Write a proposal to a streaming platform for a new series set in Colombia. Describe the premise, the genre, the target audience and why it would be successful.
5.briefEs: Escribe una propuesta a una plataforma de streaming para una nueva serie ambientada en Colombia.
criteria: Headings: Premise, Characters, Audience, Why it will work.
Two sentence adverbs and one “so…that” structure.
Use “plot twist”, “gripping” and “to suspend disbelief”.
5.model:
Proposal: "Los Guardianes del Páramo" — a six-episode thriller

Premise
When a young hydrologist arrives in a remote village in the Sumapaz páramo to study its water supply, she discovers that several local leaders have disappeared. As she investigates, she uncovers a conflict between a mining company, armed groups and an indigenous community determined to protect the largest páramo on Earth.

Characters
The protagonist, Laura, is brilliant but socially awkward, and her outsider's perspective allows viewers to discover the region through her eyes. She is joined by Don Efraín, a farmer whose knowledge of the mountains is so deep that he becomes her indispensable guide.

Audience
The series targets viewers aged 18–45 who enjoy socially conscious thrillers such as "Narcos" or "Frontera Verde", as well as international audiences interested in Latin American stories.

Why it will work
Crucially, the series combines a gripping mystery with stunning, rarely filmed landscapes. Each episode ends with a plot twist designed to keep viewers watching. Unlike many crime dramas, it never asks the audience to suspend disbelief: the story is based on real environmental conflicts, carefully researched with local experts. Interestingly, recent surveys show a growing global demand for stories about climate and nature.

Budget and timeline
We estimate filming would take four months, with a budget of USD 6 million. We would be delighted to present a full script of the pilot episode.

5.title: Overrated: a dissenting review
5.brief: Write a review of a very popular film or series that you consider overrated. Argue your position respectfully and acknowledge its strengths.
5.briefEs: Escribe una reseña de una película o serie muy popular que consideras sobrevalorada, reconociendo sus fortalezas.
criteria: Four sentence adverbs to signal stance (frankly, admittedly, curiously, regrettably).
Two “such…that” or “so…that” sentences.
Use “overrated”, “hit and miss” and “to give away”.
5.model:
It may be the most-watched series in Netflix's history, but Squid Game left me strangely cold.

Admittedly, its premise is brilliant. Hundreds of people drowning in debt are invited to compete in children's games for an enormous cash prize, only to discover that losing means death. The contrast between the brightly coloured sets and the brutal violence is so striking that the first episode is genuinely unforgettable. Lee Jung-jae, as the gambling-addicted protagonist, delivers a performance of remarkable vulnerability.

Regrettably, the series fails to sustain that early promise. After the initial shock, the structure becomes predictable: a new game, a few deaths, a moment of betrayal, repeat. The secondary storyline involving a police officer is so poorly developed that it feels like padding. Frankly, several episodes could have been cut without losing anything essential.

More importantly, the social criticism, which many viewers praised, is surprisingly superficial.
